clue.text: Steal a work by Piet Mondrian? (8)

blocks.note: a formal verb for taking something away, removing it
Mondrian painted grids of black lines and primary-colour blocks, non-representational art

explanation.surface: An art theft: someone making off with a Mondrian canvas.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as one crime, but it splits into a verb and a noun; the question mark admits the painting is only one kind of abstract.
explanation.definitionFit: To abstract is to remove or purloin, and an abstract is a non-representational painting like Mondrian's.

clue.text: In which soldiers sometimes take a dip? (6,3)

definitions.text: In which soldiers sometimes take a dip?

blocks.note: not troops: in Britain soldiers are fingers of buttered toast
the toast is dunked into a runny yolk at breakfast

explanation.surface: Troops going for a swim somewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain 'soldiers' are fingers of buttered toast, lined up like troops and dunked into the runny yolk of a boiled egg.
explanation.definitionFit: A soft-boiled egg is exactly what toast soldiers are dipped into.

clue.text: Might it deter free camping? (7)

indicators.note: camping means being in a tent, so RID goes inside TENT

blocks.note: the camper is in a TENT
to free of something is to rid; RID sits inside TENT

explanation.surface: A sign or rule aimed at stopping people pitching tents for nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Camping' does double duty, giving the shelter and saying the freeing goes inside it. Trident is the UK's submarine-launched nuclear deterrent, and peace camps have long protested at its base.
explanation.definitionFit: Trident is Britain's nuclear deterrent, so it is something that might deter.

clue.text: Daisy a stunner, lowering temperature (5)

indicators.note: in a down entry the T for temperature moves lower in the word

blocks.note: a Taser is a stun gun; in a down entry its first T moves two places lower

explanation.surface: Someone called Daisy described as a knockout who has cooled off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Daisy' looks like a woman's name and 'stunner' like a beauty; the stunner is the electric weapon.
explanation.definitionFit: Asters are daisy-like flowers of the daisy family.

clue.text: Couple from Bangkok, did you say? (3)

indicators.note: asks whether you heard it right, so the word is taken by sound

blocks.note: someone from Bangkok is Thai; say that and write the sound another way

explanation.surface: A pair of travellers who come from the Thai capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Couple' looks like a noun, a pair of people; it is the verb, to join.
explanation.definitionFit: To couple two things is to tie them together.

clue.text: A mob destroying last of Arab’s crops (6)

definitions.note: ARABLE is used as a noun for arable crops, though it is usually an adjective

indicators.note: the B is wiped out of the mob
points at the final letter of Arab's

blocks.note: taken as it stands
a rabble is a mob; it loses one B
the final letter of Arab, removed from RABBLE

explanation.surface: Rioters wrecking an Arab farmer's harvest.
explanation.walkthrough: Arable farming grows crops rather than rearing animals, and 'arable' as a noun is farmers' shorthand for those crops.
explanation.definitionFit: Arable is land or farming given to growing crops, and farmers speak of 'arable' for the crops themselves.

clue.text: Staff taken in by Saatchi & Saatchi — time to make a change? (9)

indicators.note: MEN is taken inside ADMEN

blocks.note: Saatchi & Saatchi is an advertising agency, full of admen
staff = men, the workforce; it goes inside ADMEN after the A
t = time

explanation.surface: An ad agency hires someone and decides it is time to shake things up.
explanation.walkthrough: Saatchi & Saatchi is a famous London advertising agency, so the firm stands for its admen.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a change made to a motion or law has this as its standard formal name.

clue.text: After tip off, searched vagrant in French department (7)

indicators.note: the tip, the first letter, is taken off
wandering, so the letters stray into a new order

blocks.note: searched without its tip, the S

explanation.surface: Police frisking a tramp somewhere in France.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vagrant' looks like the person searched; it is the anagram indicator. The Ardèche is a department of south-east France.
explanation.definitionFit: The Ardèche is one of France's administrative departments, named after its river.

clue.text: Magnifying glass? Ring for delivery (5)

indicators.note: delivery is speaking aloud, so take the word as spoken

blocks.note: a ring is a loop; the answer is a French-looking spelling of that sound

explanation.surface: A jeweller's lens and a ring, perhaps being sent out to a customer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Delivery' suggests a parcel; it means the way words are delivered, spoken.
explanation.definitionFit: A loupe is the small magnifying lens jewellers and watchmakers screw into the eye.

clue.text: Film in which I perform, making a comeback (4)

indicators.note: coming back means running the letters backwards

blocks.note: taken as it stands
a musician who plays a live set does this

explanation.surface: A has-been actor announcing a return in a new movie.
explanation.walkthrough: Gigi is the 1958 musical film starring Leslie Caron.
explanation.definitionFit: Gigi is a well-known film, the musical that won nine Oscars.

clue.text: Most endure somehow? That’s terrific (10)

indicators.note: in some way or other, so the letters take some other order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 10 letters

explanation.surface: Admiring the way most people get through hardship.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark and 'That's terrific' make it read as a reaction to hard times; the reaction is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Tremendous and terrific both mean excellent, and both once meant frightening.

clue.text: Famous Scot almost rebuked by English bishop (10)

indicators.note: cuts the last letter off CELT

blocks.note: a Scot is a Celt, missing its final T
E = English
B = bishop in chess notation
to rate someone is an old word for scolding them

explanation.walkthrough: 'Famous Scot' reads as one phrase, but 'Famous' is the definition. RATED meaning scolded survives in 'berate'.
explanation.definitionFit: Celebrated means famous, widely praised.

clue.text: Some complain at Italy holding back drama queen (7)

indicators.note: only some of the clue's letters are used
the words hold the answer, written backwards

blocks.note: the run compl(AIN AT IT)aly, read backwards

explanation.surface: A theatrical diva moaning about Italy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drama queen' suggests a diva; it is a queen from a play. Titania is queen of the fairies in A Midsummer Night's Dream.
explanation.definitionFit: Titania is the fairy queen in Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream, a queen in a drama.

clue.text: Singer dear to Jean-Paul Sartre (4)

blocks.note: the American pop star known by one name
the French word for dear, the one Sartre would use

explanation.surface: A singer whom the French philosopher held dear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dear to' looks like fondness; Sartre only signals French.
explanation.definitionFit: One word covers both halves: the one-name pop star, and the French for dear.

clue.text: Feeling thrilled to host new match (8)

indicators.note: SENT holds the rest inside it

blocks.note: sent = thrilled, carried away; it opens between N and T
a tie is a cup match
n = new

explanation.surface: Excitement at staging a fresh fixture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Feeling thrilled' reads as one phrase; 'Feeling' is the adjective definition. A tie is a knockout match, as in the FA Cup.
explanation.definitionFit: An adjective for able to perceive or feel, so a feeling creature is a sentient one.

clue.text: One who left you now feeling the strain, reportedly — such is life! (9)

indicators.note: as reported, by word of mouth, so take the sound

blocks.note: your ex is a former partner who left
someone feeling the strain now is tense

explanation.surface: A jilted lover sighing that that's how things go.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Such is life!' looks like a shrug at the end; 'life' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: being alive, the state of being, as in 'a miserable existence'.

clue.text: Shutter closed for siesta? (6)

blocks.note: not on a window: the shutter is a flap of skin over the eye
it comes down when you nod off in the afternoon

explanation.surface: A Spanish window shuttered for the afternoon rest.
explanation.walkthrough: The shutter looks like one on a window in a hot country; it is the one over your eye.
explanation.definitionFit: An eyelid shuts over the eye like a shutter, and it closes when you sleep.

clue.text: Ice storm raging round island of same size (9)

indicators.note: wild, so the letters are thrown about
the letters go round the I

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 8 letters
I = island, joined to the fodder

explanation.surface: A blizzard battering an island.
explanation.walkthrough: The weather picture hides a technical adjective at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Isometric means having equal dimensions or measurements.

clue.text: A soldier eating blooming rodent! (6)

indicators.note: what eats something takes it inside, so GI swallows OUT

blocks.note: taken as it stands
a GI is an American soldier
flowers in bloom are out

explanation.surface: A soldier chewing on a flipping rat!
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blooming' looks like the mild British swear-word; it means in flower. An agouti is a South American rodent.
explanation.definitionFit: The agouti is a long-legged rodent of Central and South America.

clue.text: Union leader quietly taken out and briefed (7)

indicators.note: the leading, first, letter of Union

blocks.note: first letter of Union
p = piano, quietly
someone taken out on a date has been dated

explanation.surface: A trade union boss being discreetly removed and then given instructions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Taken out' suggests removal or worse; it means taken out for dinner.
explanation.definitionFit: Being briefed means being given the latest information, which is being brought up to date.

clue.text: Computer discovered in Spooner’s secluded spot on ship (8)

indicators.note: swap the opening sounds, as Rev. Spooner did

blocks.note: a ship, loosely, is a boat; it hands its B over and takes the N
a nook is a secluded corner; it takes the B

explanation.surface: A laptop turned up in a hidden corner of a vessel.
explanation.walkthrough: The Rev. William Spooner, an Oxford don, swapped the starts of words; 'on ship' puts the vessel first.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: this is a small, light laptop, one kind of computer.

clue.text: Spirit of a royal house (7)

blocks.note: a spirit here is a strong drink, an American corn whiskey
the dynasty that ruled France and Spain

explanation.surface: The ghost that haunts a palace.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spirit' reads as a ghost; it is the drink.

clue.text: Briefly compelled to accommodate initially intransigent spinster (4)

indicators.note: cut short by its last letter
MAD gives the I house room
first letter of intransigent

blocks.note: made = compelled, cut short
first letter of intransigent

explanation.surface: A stubborn single woman being forced to put someone up.
explanation.walkthrough: Maid in the old sense of an unmarried woman, as in 'old maid'.

clue.text: Doctor in casualty first to recognise warning sign (5)

indicators.note: 'in' places the doctor inside casualty, MB inside AE
the first letter of recognise

MB, Bachelor of Medicine, is a doctor's degree
first letter of recognise

clue.text: Stupidly trusted man touched by alchemy? (10)

explanation.walkthrough: The alchemist's goal was to transmute base metals into gold; the question mark flags the fanciful definition.

clue.text: Mean to go without Penny? (5)

clue.text: Self-restraint sent most of cabinet mad (10)

cabinet without its last T

clue.text: Peter maybe given tip — the best one? (3)

clue.text: Take offence, left in second-class transport (6)

clue.text: Sweet kiss, a comfort in the cooler months? (4,4)
